571.quote_or_event: “The function of the souls (jīva) is to help one another.”
571.explanation: Umasvati's aphorism parasparopagraho jivanam, now treated as a motto of Jainism, says that living beings exist in a web of mutual help.
571.tie_back: The Kural says the world keeps going because kindly regard for others exists; the Jain sutra likewise makes mutual help the defining function of every soul.
571.source: Tattvartha Sutra 5.21 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
571._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib. Pujyapada's gloss also notes that beings cause each other pain, so the sutra describes mutual dependence as much as kindness.

572.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
572.explanation: The four bhavanas (contemplations) of friendliness, joy, compassion and equanimity are given to sustain the vows of non-violence and the rest.
572.tie_back: The Kural says all the world's business runs on kindly regard; the Jain sutra makes goodwill toward every being a daily discipline underlying all conduct.
572.source: Tattvartha Sutra 7.11 (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
572._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Vijay K. Jain's translation on wisdomlib. Strong thematic fit, but the Kural's verdict that people without this are a burden on the earth is not in the sutra.

573.quote_or_event: The Dasavaikalika Sutra's maxim padhamam nanam tao daya, 'first knowledge, then compassion', teaches that knowledge exists for the sake of compassion toward living beings.
573.explanation: Jain teaching sees knowing and seeing as incomplete until they lead to compassion (daya).
573.tie_back: The Kural asks what use an eye is without kindly regard; the Jain maxim likewise treats knowing without compassion as missing its purpose.
573.source: Dasavaikalika Sutra 4.10 (as quoted and translated on the Jainstudy blog)
573._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from a secondary blog rendering because no primary translation was checked in this session; the Kural's music image (melody without song) has no Jain counterpart.

574.quote_or_event: “Though he may possess all five organs of sense, still it is a rare chance to be instructed in the best Law; for people follow heretical teachers”
574.explanation: Mahavira tells Gautama that having complete senses is not enough unless they lead a person to the true Law.
574.tie_back: The Kural says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be in the face; the Jain verse likewise says faculties in themselves count for little until they serve something higher.
574.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.18 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
574._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A next-best match: it concerns the rarity of hearing the Law, not kindness, and the idea of 'due measure' is absent.

575.quote_or_event: “As you look so happy in outward appearance, you must have peace of mind.”
575.explanation: A former Kshatriya who has turned monk reads Sanjaya's inner peace from the brightness of his face.
575.tie_back: The Kural calls kindly regard the jewel of the eye; the Jain verse likewise assumes that a person's inner quality shows in, and adorns, the face.
575.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 18.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
575._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. A weak next-best match: there is no ornament or wound image, and peace of mind is not kindness.

576.quote_or_event: Jain teaching classes plants among the ekendriya beings, souls that possess only one sense, touch; human birth with all five senses is counted a rare chance that should not be wasted.
576.explanation: In Jain cosmology a tree is a living soul limited to a single sense, while a human being has the full faculties needed for right conduct.
576.tie_back: The Kural compares people who have eyes but show no kindly regard to trees standing in the soil; on Jain terms, such a person lives with five senses but, morally, no better than a one-sensed being.
576.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 10.5-9 and 10.17, with Jacobi's note on the ekendriyas (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
576._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from verses and a footnote checked on sacred-texts.com. The comparison is my own interpretive bridge, and Jainism respects plants as living souls rather than using them as a figure of insensibility.

577.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
577.explanation: Mahavira's road to deliverance begins with right vision or faith (samyag-darshana), without which nothing else counts as true knowing or right action.
577.tie_back: The Kural says that those without kindly regard are really eyeless; Jainism likewise separates physical sight from right 'seeing' (darshana), which alone counts as true vision.
577.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 28.30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
577._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's footnote markers omitted). Jain right vision is faith in the true categories of reality, not kindness, so the parallel is structural.

578.quote_or_event: “Virodhi Himsa is the kind of injury which is necessarily committed in defense of person and property, against thieves, robbers, dacoits, assailants and enemies, in meeting their aggression, and in causing the least possible injury, necessary in the circumstances, in which one may find oneself.”
578.explanation: Jain lay ethics requires a householder to give up intentional violence but recognises that protecting people and property may require force, always kept to the least possible injury.
578.tie_back: The Kural says the world belongs to those who are kind without letting their duty suffer; Jain ethics likewise lets the householder, or the ruler, do the duty of protection while keeping the injury done to a minimum.
578.source: 'The Concept of Himsa', Jain philosophy pages on jainworld.com
578._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on jainworld.com, a modern secondary exposition rather than scripture. It is about necessary force rather than favouritism versus justice, so the fit is partial.

579.quote_or_event: “Ceasing to use the stick (i.e. cruelty) against living beings, abandoning the care of the body, the houseless (Mahâvîra), the Venerable One, endures the thorns of the villages (i.e. the abusive language of the peasants), (being) perfectly enlightened.”
579.explanation: In the pathless Ladha country villagers beat Mahavira, set dogs on him and abused him, and he bore it all without retaliating.
579.tie_back: The Kural ranks forbearing kindness toward those who hurt us as the highest virtue; Mahavira's patience under the Ladha villagers' blows and insults is the Jain model of that forbearance.
579.source: Acaranga Sutra I.9.3.7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; wisdomlib.org, where it is numbered Lecture 8, Lesson 3)
579._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on wisdomlib (which numbers the lectures differently because the seventh is lost). This is endurance and non-retaliation rather than active kindness, but it is very close.

580.quote_or_event: The monk Dharmaruchi, breaking a month-long fast, was served a dish of bitter gourd that his teacher recognised as deadly; sent to dispose of it, he saw ants die after touching a drop, and rather than let more creatures die he ate the whole poisonous dish himself and died calmly.
580.explanation: This story, from the Jnatadharmakatha tradition, shows a monk knowingly swallowing poison he has seen served to him rather than cause harm.
580.tie_back: The Kural praises those who calmly drink poison they have seen poured; Dharmaruchi does this literally, though his motive is compassion for small beings rather than courtesy toward a friend.
580.source: Dharmaruchi Muni story (Jnatadharmakatha tradition), as retold on jainworld.com
580._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the jainworld.com retelling (names of the cook vary between versions). The poison is served carelessly rather than by a friend, and the motive is ahimsa rather than preserving a friendship.
